story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm sharing a game I've been building for the last few months.

You run a tech company, starting with a few engineers and a Monolith. Requirements earn revenue, revenue unlocks funding, and funding hires more engineers. Let tech debt pile up or morale slide, and your engineers get less done, or quit. Once someone IPOs, a clock starts and the highest valuation wins. Or you can win the AI Race.

I've been an engineer in tech for a long time. I was aiming for something that allowed me to visually represent a software stack like you see or build at modern tech companies. I also wanted something tongue-in-cheek about the silly things we say (YAGNI, KISS) and the shitty things that happen at companies (layoffs, audits), but deep enough for real strategy. Inspired by some of my faves: Lichess, MTG, Twilight Struggle, Slay the Spire, Balatro.

You can play a tutorial, a bot, pass-and-play, or the online arena: ranked matches or private rooms with friends. You can also create an account and connect agents which play in their own lane over MCP. Pipe dream: Monolith becomes a new benchmark for AI releases.

Tech stack: TypeScript/Node (for now; rust rewrite of the engine is on the table...). Matches stream over server-sent events, and the same rules engine runs the server and the bots.

Feedback is much appreciated, here or via Report a bug in the menu. I'm especially curious whether the first few turns make sense.

story_text.value:
Howdy HN!

Missing a fast pure Go embedded SQL database. The issue is that compared to C, go is slow. Having done a lot of JIT in go, I naturally wanted to stick a JIT that generates native query kernels and see what happens.

Result: musql. Pronounced "muscle."

On a 100K-row filtered count, musql takes 21 µs: about 300x faster than C SQLite and nearly 1,000x faster than Turso. Single-threaded, warm cache, using musql's direct API, native C SQLite, and Turso's Go driver. Filtered sums are 130x faster than C SQLite, grouped aggregates 95x.

It works with Go's database/sql or through a server for libSQL clients. It uses its own storage format, with SQLite import/export. And yes, the SQL VM runs DOOM.

Code, setup, and benchmarks: https://github.com/samyfodil/musql

story_text.value:
I'm obsessed with Egyptology. During covid, I wanted to get a hieratic tattoo. For those who don't know, hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs that was used in day-to-day life in ancient Egypt. It's as old as hieroglyphs.

I then went on a mission to have a sentence translated into hieratic. Luckily, in 2022, I was able to commission an Oxford Egyptologist to write it for me. After that, I took it to a hieratic specialist I found on Instagram to redraw it with "biblical" accuracy.

When generative AI came out, I realized that models very rarely identify hieratic and almost never translate it correctly. Every single time a new model came out, I ended up testing my sentence and hieratic texts in general, and I realized this could actually become a benchmark. Since so many benchmarks are becoming saturated, we need to find weird ways to test new models.

That's why I decided to build HieraticBench.

The first version of the benchmark has 268 items, including real documents, signs, and other Egyptian scripts, which I used as controls, as well as my unpublished sentence in two different renditions. The current state-of-the-art foundation models are hilariously bad at identifying my sentence, especially the one the Egyptologist wrote with her pen. Some of them said Tibetan, Urdu, Korean, and, funnily enough, "Reformed Egyptian," which is from the Book of Mormon.

On real documents, the best model in the benchmark identified hieratic correctly 95% of the time, and the best score for reading individual signs was around 13%. That's when we tell the model specifically that it's hieratic. None of them can really translate a sealed sentence that's never been published and has no answer key.

I haven't run every model on every task just to keep costs down. My next steps were to run Astra and Gemini 3.1 Pro on real documents. Currently, only the Claude models have done the sign readings.

And just FYI, I have no experience whatsoever running benchmarks or evaluations, so not 100% sure I scored things right.

Things we need: - Running the models I haven't covered - More sealed sentences and labeled signs

If you know hieratic or have an Egyptologist friend, reach out at hieraticbench@veeza.ai.

Source code: https://github.com/alymoursy/hieraticbench

I'll be around to answer questions.

story_text.value:
Claude has a way of talking. Most people I work with are tired of it, me included. Call it Claude-speak.

It opens with "Great question" and a header. The answer hides in the middle. It reaches for a metaphor when a plain phrase would do: "a 3,000-line merge gets a skim and a prayer". It explains with a contrast instead of a reason: "this is intent, not behavior". It drops a slogan: "the decision is the feature". It recaps what it just did. It ends with "happy to dig further if useful". An engineering question gets 500 to 600 words of this.

Terse is 22 writing rules as a forced output style. First sentence is the answer. One idea per sentence. A number or a name in every claim. No slogans, no reframes, no closing offers. 150 words, unless you ask for a document. A hook re-sends a short digest with every prompt, so the rules hold at turn 30.

Same 20 prompts, same codebase, with and without the plugin: Opus 5.5 went from 9,705 words to 4,468 at 32% lower cost. Fable 5.1 wrote 46% fewer words. One prompt in the README: 636 words before, 180 after.

One rule failed. A ban on first person passed every benchmark and lost in daily use. Half my real replies still said "I'll tell you when the compile finishes". The benchmark never asked Claude to act as an agent. Details in docs/benchmark.md.

Claude plugin directory, search "terse". Or /plugin marketplace add lowenbjer/claude-terse. MIT. If it still writes Claude-speak, post the reply as an issue. There's a template.

story_text.value:
I built Banyan, a procedural banyan tree in a single HTML file. Every tree grows from a 32-bit seed and nothing is downloaded.

There is a banyan in front of my house, and I always wanted one that comes out different for every seed. I started the three.js version in July this year. ez-tree was an influence along the way.

I measured a benchmark test against ez-tree july end. Banyan led on silhouette, wood and foliage whereas ez-tree led on materials and presentation.

Everything in the scene is generated from code: the trunk, aerial prop roots, bark, leaves, ground, grass, litter and light. The file is about 748 KB with three.js r165 bundled in, and it makes no network requests.

The hardest problem was performance on phones. I moved five noise fields from the pixel shader to the vertex shader. That helped on my laptop but made things worse on my iPhone 13, because the trunk has about 125,000 vertices and covers fewer pixels than that at the opening view. Moving work to the vertex shader only pays when there are fewer vertices than pixels covered. The fields are now baked once on the GPU when the tree is built.

At the balanced tier, a seed always gives the same geometry. Pixels can differ because the bark is baked on your GPU and auto mode may pick a lighter tier on a small screen. I picked ten seeds out of 2400 candidates and recorded their digests, and the README has a console snippet that checks seed 863 against them. 'npm run check' rebuilds the file and checks it against the published hash and CI runs the same check on Linux and Windows.

It is banyan-inspired, not botanical that is, one trunk, age fixed at 100 years, at most 12 prop roots and wind as vertex sway.

If you have stood under a real banyan, I would like to know how far off the geometry, shape and foliage are.

Source: https://github.com/satyasairay/banyan

PS: Built it solo, with AI agents since July 2026.

story_text.value:
Paganel comes from an old work problem: I had a large schema migration with lots of transformations and several environments to check. One of the main requirements was to validate whether the data had moved correctly, and I was not allowed to use any SaaS tools because it was forbidden for data to leave our network. Since I couldn't find any air-gapped tool that could do both the transformation and the verification (basic row counts aren't enough for transformed data), I had to write custom scripts for the entire process.

Ever since then, the idea of automating complex migrations has stuck in my head, which led me to start building Paganel a year and a half ago.

In Paganel, a migration is just a single declarative file. You specify where the data comes from and where it's going, and the rest goes in the same file: joins, filters, computed fields, and validation rules.

If you are missing a specific source, sink, transform, or filter, you can easily extend Paganel by writing your own WASM plugin in Rust or JS. These execute inside a strict sandbox, so they don't have any filesystem or network access unless you allow it in the migration config.

I also wanted to make large migrations simple, so before running a real migration, you can run pag plan to review the output schema, the DDL, and the time and memory estimates. You can also use the plan to see a sample of real rows. They get processed through the whole pipeline, which gives you absolute clarity on what will actually be inserted.

One of the biggest challenges isn't just doing the migration, but verifying that everything actually moved correctly. For that, there is the --integrity flag. Pass it, and Paganel hashes the rows on the fly as they migrate, storing those hashes on disk, keyed by primary key. After the run, it uses them to spit out a 32-byte root hash for the table. Together with the row hashes, this gives you a complete 'migration receipt.'

Minutes or weeks later, you can run pag verify, and it re-reads the destination, recomputes the hashes and compares them with the receipt, without connecting to the source. When the root doesn't match, you know something changed, and then verify goes through the row hashes and tells you which rows it was.

It tells you that the destination still contains what Paganel wrote, but it can't tell you whether the transformation itself was correct.

Another huge factor is migration speed. I created a small benchmark to measure Paganel's speed and tested it on a 100M-row migration from MySQL to PostgreSQL (with the databases on separate servers). With the default config, which is a single stream, I got about 390k rows a second. Splitting the table into four parallel streams got it to almost 940k. The number of streams is configurable for tables with an integer primary key. Enabling the --integrity flag does add some overhead, dropping those numbers to 340k and 670k, respectively.

Paganel is still pre-v1.0, so there are some rough edges to be aware of:

- No CDC yet: Currently, it only handles batch processing. Continuous sync with verification is the ultimate goal, but nailing the batch engine comes first.

- Limited databases: Right now, Paganel only natively supports MySQL and PostgreSQL.

- API changes: The project is under heavy development, meaning the config syntax might change slightly from release to release.

- One-man team: I'm developing this solo. You will likely run into edge cases I haven't caught yet.

- Platform testing: The full integration suite and all my own manual testing run on Linux. macOS and Windows get pre-built binaries too, but they only go through a basic smoke test.

If you want to try it out, the quickstart in the README will spin up some sample databases in Docker for you.

How do you verify migrations today? I'd like to know whether a receipt like this would fit into how you work.

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Today, we're launching selfbench.dev, an open-source tool that lets you create and run evals automatically from your PRs.

Every benchmark with sufficient trust eventually gets benchmaxxed (Goodhart's law) - the labs are incentivized to maximize their scores on that benchmark, which isn't predictive on whether it'll actually work within your setup. This has been a time-consuming process that only the largest companies can afford to do, so we built self-bench to fix this.

Self-bench uses agents to author / review Harbor environments generated from your PRs. You then approve every eval that the agent created, and can model/harness evals concurrently on sandboxes.

To save you money, we also allow you to connect your OpenAI and Claude subscriptions so you don't have to pay raw token costs.

We ran evals on several large codebases like

- Posthog (https://selfbench.dev/PostHog/posthog)

- Next.js (https://selfbench.dev/vercel/next.js)

- Sentry (https://selfbench.dev/getsentry/sentry)

- Pi (https://selfbench.dev/earendil-works/pi)

- as well as other fantastic open-source projects (all on selfbench.dev)

From our evals:

- Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 are almost always more expensive, yet less performant than models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, due to token efficiency.

- GPT-6 Luna is almost always the most effective "cost-efficient" model we've tested, not open-source models.

We'd love for you to try this on your codebase and let us know what you think!

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built and open-sourced Carve to handle repetitive work in windows you already use.

Choose the window in any Mac app where you want it to work, press Option-D, and watch it do what you want. For example, in the demo I show an example CRM and Carve entering contact details and drafting a follow up. It also has the ability to annotate and explain items on the screen.

This runs with your own API keys, and can even support OpenRouter, though OpenAI is the best tested. Experimental adapters also for Bedrock, Azure. No reason it couldn't expand beyond experimental support to support more local models.

I built this because I found that Claude and Codex were rather clunky when using computer use, I like having a sleek window that just pops up and shows me what it's doing. Also it has the 3 similar modes (approve plan, step by step manual approval, or act directly mode).

Local currently covers browser actions via vision models, computer use support is required for operating other native mac apps. This is an ongoing area of work.

I'm seeing a lot of demand for local model support and building out relevant tooling so wanted to contribute. We're just now at the point where models are getting fast and smart enough to make rapid computer use possible. You can take a look at the benchmarks in the repository, Carve currently can rapidly and cheaply handle explaining, summarizing, basic navigation, and extraction. Complex, long horizon tasks are a work in progress, though I'm seeing promising results. Failures resemble patterns, and you can identify patterns and fix them by running evaluations in batches.

I'd love any feedback on how well the tool works, what you tried, and any issues that you found. Thank you!

story_text.value:
I started Solarite several years ago because I wanted something simpler to use than the existing js ui frameworks. Features like:

- not having to setup a build environment or wait for compilation

- no signals or other dance to setup my data

- class based components, where I could pass arguments to sub-components as constructor args

- scoped styles, two-way binding and other nice to haves.

- not having the limitations of shadow dom (Lit)

- Just be a library I can import anywhere, not be a whole framework.

I wasn't able to find anything that did all of the above. It has a score of 1.08 on the js-framework-benchmark, which is faster than just about every widely known competitor, and most of the faster ones have implementation note "penalties" for not conforming to the benchmark requirements.

Source: https://github.com/eric-frost/solarite Docs: https://eric-frost.github.io/solarite/docs/ Js-Framework-Benchmark: https://krausest.github.io/js-framework-benchmark/current.ht...

I've used Solarite in production for a few years on a large internal work project, but I could use more feedback on the API before I feel comfortable releasing version 1.0.

story_text.value: I wanted an easily deployable way of bringing transcription to an underpowered server I have. I used Moondream's excellent parakeet-redux as a base model and adapted Highway SIMD to run it. The result is a single binary with the model embedded than can provide nearly identical transcription quality while running even faster than the Photon/torch model on CPU targets. Benchmarks are in the repository.

title.value: Show HN: Parakeetogo, a portable ASR binary faster than Photon/torch for CPU

story_text.value:
Basically, I didn't want to waste my opus 5.5 or codex Astra credits just to find files in my machine, so I trained a local LLM which is only 1.5B to write bash to find files on your macos laptop (works on apple silicon, uses little ram).

Full privacy since it's local so you can look for your sensitive files and api keys without sending them to a third party server.

It outperforms strong cloud models like Gemini 3.8 Flash and hefty 31B Param Gemma models in the file search benchmark I created to measure competency, details here: https://shlexball.com/findbench/

title.value: Show HN: Shlexball, describe a file and a local 1.5B model finds it on your Mac
